To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) if the discriminated group has no taste for discrimination, the discriminating group gains if it is made worse off, and (2) if the discriminating group has a taste for discrimination, it gains from having a taste and the discriminated group loses from being discriminated against.
Becker's welfare theorems are not valid when discrimination is defined as the result of a taste for discrimination and not as a result of a taste of favoritism.
the Becker theorems are reversed when discrimination is defined in terms of psychic benefits and that the theorems are not necessarily true when psychic costs are involved.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the welfare implications of the assumption of a discrimination coefficient.
the welfare implications of the assumption of psychic costs of discrimination.
the welfare consequences of discrimination.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Becker's results depend on whether the discriminated-against group has a “taste for discrimination” or a “taste against discrimination.”
the welfare effects of discrimination depend on whether the discrimination is in favor of or against the group doing the discriminating.

Becker's results are valid only if the discriminating group incurs a psychic cost from discriminating and that if the discriminating groups incur a psychic benefit from discriminating the group which is the target of discrimination is always worse off.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Becker’s results depend critically on the sign of the discrimination coefficient, which he assumed positive.
the welfare implications of discrimination depend critically on the nature of the discriminator.
Becker's results do not hold when the psychic costs of discrimination are not assumed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
discrimination may be welfare improving.
the results of the Becker model depend on the assumption that the discriminator is made to feel bad when he discriminates.
discrimination is always harmful to the group discriminated, but the welfare of “discriminatory” groups is ambiguous.
